subject: Gregory the Great

text_used.text: Gregory's letters and Pastoral Rule are checked against James Barmby's translation (NPNF 2nd series vols. 12 and 13, 1895 and 1898), downloaded whole from CCEL as plain text and marked Public Domain. The Moralia on Job is the Oxford Library of the Fathers translation (1844-1850), from the lectionarycentral.com transcription. The Dialogues are the English of 'P.W.' (Paris, 1608) as re-edited by Edmund G. Gardner (London, 1911), from tertullian.org. Bede is A. M. Sellar's revised translation (1907, Project Gutenberg 38326). Gregory of Tours is Ernest Brehaut's translation (1916, Fordham). Paul the Deacon's History of the Lombards is W. D. Foulke's (1907). The Whitby Life is T. Leo Almond's partial English (Downside Review, 1904) and Gasquet's Latin edition (1904). Latin: Migne PL 75 and 76 (archive.org OCR). Scholarship: F. Homes Dudden, Gregory the Great (2 vols, 1905). 'exact' is the text as printed; 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God.
text_used.source: CCEL npnf212.txt and npnf213.txt; lectionarycentral.com; tertullian.org; Gutenberg; archive.org
text_used.note: New Advent's copies of Barmby are revised (thee/thy become you/your; 'shewing' becomes 'showing'). The quiz lines on the site follow New Advent (e.g. 'under your sway'); CCEL has 'under thy sway'. Pick one form per page. All quotations below were run by script against the fetched texts in design/saints-hub/sources/people/gregory-the-great/ (see quote_checks). Several texts are OCR (archive.org): Latin quotations keep the OCR spelling in 'exact' (e.g. 'elcphas' for 'elephas') and give the corrected form in 'display'.

born.text: Born about 540 in Rome, into a rich senatorial family. His father was Gordianus, his mother Silvia.
born.source: Britannica ('born c. 540, Rome'); Merriam-Webster ('circa 540-604'); Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1 ('one of the first senatorial families'); Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1 ('son of Gordianus'); Whitby Life, chapter 1 ('whose father was Gordianus and his mother Silvia')
born.note: No ancient source gives the year. 'About 540' is the modern reckoning (Britannica, CE, OCA, LFF 2022). CE: his father was 'probably of the famous gens Anicia' (the CE text prints 'Amicia'); Britannica: he 'may have shared distant links to gens Anicia'. Leave the Anicii out, or say 'possibly'.

grew_up.text: Grew up in Rome during the wars between the Goths and the Eastern emperor. The family house stood on the Caelian Hill. He was well schooled: Gregory of Tours says no one in Rome was thought his better in grammar, rhetoric and logic.
grew_up.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1; CE, 'Pope St. Gregory I' (Rome taken and retaken between 546 and 552; mansion on the Caelian Hill); Britannica ('His family held the Caelian Hill')
grew_up.note: Exact (Brehaut): 'He was so versed in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric that he was believed second to none in the city.' He never learned Greek: CE, 'he seems never to have mastered even the rudiments of Greek'; Britannica, 'remained ignorant of Greek'. (azbyka.ru says he studied Greek in Byzantium: the Western sources disagree; follow CE and Britannica.)

died.text: Died on 12 March 604 in Rome, about 64 years old, after years of gout and fever.
died.source: Dudden, Gregory the Great (1905), vol. 2, p. 268 ('His release came on the 12th of March, 604'); Whitby Life, chapter 32 ('the fourth day before the ides of March'); Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 (burial 'on the 12th day of March'); Britannica ('died March 12, 604, Rome'); CE ('The end came on 12 March, 604'); his own letters on gout (Book 9, letter 123; Book 10, letter 35; Book 14, letter 12)
died.note: Bede puts the death in 605 ('At this time, that is, in the year of our Lord 605'). Dudden says Bede 'wrongly gives the date 605'; Foulke's note to Paul the Deacon: 'Paul, following Bede as his authority, errs as to this date'. Fordham's older translation of Bede renders 'die quarto Iduum Martiarum' as '4th day of March': that is a mistranslation; the Latin means 12 March (Sellar prints 12 March). Cause: no source names a single cause. His last letters speak of gout so bad he could hardly speak (Book 14, letter 12, late 603). saint.gr says he died 'από αρθριτική νόσο' (of arthritic disease). Say 'after years of illness, above all gout'.

buried.text: Buried the same day in the porch of St Peter's in Rome, in front of the sacristy. His body now lies under an altar inside St Peter's.
buried.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 ('buried in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter before the sacristy'); Dudden vol. 2, p. 268 ('on the same day he was buried in the portico of the Basilica of St. Peter, in front of the sacristy'); CE (moved several times, last by Paul V in 1606); Britannica (caption: 'Altar of St. Gregory the Great in St. Peter's Basilica ... Gregory's body is beneath the mosaic altarpiece')
buried.note: Dudden says the remains rest 'beneath the altar in the Chapel of Clement the Eighth'; CE says Paul V placed them 'in the chapel of Clement V' (a slip for Clement VIII). Say 'under an altar in St Peter's' and leave the chapel's name out. OCA: 'his relics rest in the cathedral of the holy Apostle Peter in the Vatican'.

also_called.text: Gregory the Great (Latin Gregorius Magnus); Pope Gregory I.
also_called.source: Merriam-Webster ('I Saint circa 540-604 the Great (pope 590-604)'); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 12 March ('surnamed the Great')

also_called.text: Gregory the Dialogist, or Gregory Dialogus, in the Orthodox Church, after his book of Dialogues. Greek: Γρηγόριος ο Διάλογος. Russian: Григорий Двоеслов.
also_called.source: OCA, 'Saint Gregory Dialogus, Pope of Rome' ('After the appearance of his book, DIALOGUES ... the saint was called “Dialogus.”'); saint.gr 3826 ('Όσιος Γρηγόριος ο Α' Διάλογος Πάπας Ρώμης'); azbyka.ru ('Святитель Григорий Двоеслов, Великий')
also_called.note: Greek synaxaria give him the monk's title Hosios (Venerable) as well; the Russian calendar gives the bishop's title Svyatitel (Holy Hierarch).

also_called.text: The Apostle of the English (Bede: 'we may rightly, nay, we must, call him our apostle'). The 1916 Roman Martyrology: 'called the Apostle of England'.
also_called.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 (Sellar); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 12 March; LFF 2022 ('Bede justly called Gregory "The Apostle of the English."')

also_called.text: He called himself 'servant of the servants of God' (servus servorum Dei). Many of his letters open with it.
also_called.source: Letters, Book 1, letter 1 ('Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Sicily'); Britannica ('He called himself “servant of the servants of God.”')
also_called.note: Whether he was the first pope to use it was not checked. Say 'he called himself', not 'he invented'.

status.text: A saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church. Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day.
status.source: CE, 'Doctors of the Church' ('four eminent Fathers of the Church attained this honour in the early Middle Ages: St. Gregory the Great, St. Ambrose, St. Augustine, and St. Jerome'); USCCB ('Memorial of Saint Gregory the Great, Pope and Doctor of the Church'); OCA; CofE; LFF 2022; LCMS; ELW
status.note: CE, 'Pope St. Gregory I': 'His canonization by popular acclamation followed at once on his death'. The Whitby Life (about 704-714): 'that always, by all and everywhere, he is called St. Gregory' (Almond).

patron_of.text: Britannica lists teachers, students, singers, musicians, people with epilepsy, and England.
patron_of.source: Britannica, 'St. Gregory the Great' quick facts ('Patron saint of: Educators, students, singers, musicians, people with epilepsy, England')
patron_of.note: The 1916 Roman Martyrology's patron list has no entry for him. Dudden (vol. 2, p. 271, note 1) found an old Belgian custom: schoolboys started their alphabet on his feast, and he was called 'patronus addiscentium litteras' (patron of those learning letters). The music patronage rests on the chant legend (see misquoted_or_legend). Print Britannica's list with 'Britannica lists', not as a church decree.

in_art.text: Most often shown as a pope, in full vestments with the papal tiara and a double cross, with a dove, the sign of the Holy Spirit, at his ear or head.
in_art.source: CE ('In art the great pope is usually shown in full pontifical robes with the tiara and double cross. A dove is his special emblem'); Britannica (ivory book cover c. 980 showing him 'receiving information from the Holy Spirit, represented as a dove')
in_art.note: The dove comes from a later story (see miracles). Goya's painting (the band picture) shows him writing in tiara and cope, without the dove.

in_art.text: Also in the 'Mass of St Gregory': Christ appearing over the altar while he says Mass.
in_art.source: Commons category 'Mass of Saint Gregory'; Dudden vol. 2, p. 272 (the legend of the mass of Gregory)
in_art.note: The late-medieval image grew out of the Whitby Life's story of the bread (see miracles), but the early story has no vision of Christ. The art history of the image was not checked in a source; describe it only by what the paintings show.

in_art.text: In Eastern icons: a bishop with a white omophorion marked with crosses, holding a scroll or a book, named 'the Dialogist'.
in_art.source: The 17th-century Cretan icon from the Savvathiana monastery (Collection of Agia Aikaterini, Heraklion), the second picture below
in_art.note: From looking at the icon only; no written source on Eastern iconography of Gregory was checked.

wrote.text: The Pastoral Rule (a handbook for pastors); the Moralia, 35 books on Job; four books of Dialogues on the saints of Italy (Book 2 is the only early life of St Benedict); 40 homilies on the Gospels; 22 on Ezekiel; and 14 books of letters.
wrote.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 ('five and thirty books', 'forty homilies on the Gospel', 'four books of Dialogues', 'twenty-two homilies' on Ezekiel, 'private letters'); CE ('Moralium Libri XXXV'; 'Regulae Pastoralis Liber'; 'Dialogorum Libri IV'; 'Homiliarum in Ezechielem Prophetam Libri II'; 'Homiliarum in Evangelia Libri II'; 'Epistolarum Libri XIV' 'now admitted as genuine on all hands')
wrote.note: OCA counts 848 surviving letters ('His letters (848)'); no other fetched source gives a count. CE lists works once credited to him but 'almost certainly spurious' (on 1 Kings, the Song of Songs, the seven penitential psalms). A few modern scholars doubt that he wrote the Dialogues; no source for that was fetched (see could_not_verify).

pronounced.note: The MW entry is the one that covers 'I Saint circa 540-604 the Great (pope 590-604)'.

roles.text: Prefect of Rome: the city's chief civil officer, about 573, when he was little more than thirty.
roles.source: CE ('about the year 573, when little more than thirty years old, filling the important office of prefect of the city of Rome'); Britannica ('573, when Gregory became urban prefect'); Barmby, Prolegomena, NPNF 12 ('Prætor Urbanus')
roles.note: Gregory of Tours: 'he who had been used to arrayed in silken robes and glittering jewels was now clad in cheap garments' (Brehaut's English, sic).

roles.text: Monk: about 574 he gave his wealth away, founded six monasteries in Sicily and turned his family house in Rome into St Andrew's monastery, where he lived as a monk.
roles.source: Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1; CE ('This event took place most probably in 574'); Britannica

roles.text: Deacon and papal envoy at the emperor's court in Constantinople, from about 579 to 585 or 586.
roles.source: CE ('the spring of 579 ... lasted apparently for about six years'; 'In the year 586, or possibly 585, he was recalled'); Britannica ('In 579 ... apocrisiarius ... In 585-586 he returned')
roles.note: CE and the Whitby Life say he became abbot of St Andrew's on his return; Britannica says 'nor does evidence exist that Gregory became abbot'. Leave 'abbot' out, or say 'some say abbot'.

roles.text: Pope from 3 September 590 until his death on 12 March 604.
roles.source: Britannica ('Reign as pope: September 3, 590-March 12, 604'); Dudden vol. 1, p. 222 ('The event took place on the 3rd day of September, in the year of our Lord 590'); Bede ('thirteen years, six months, and ten days')

roles.text: Writer and teacher: a Doctor of the Church, whose books were the textbooks of the Middle Ages.
roles.source: CE ('his writings became to a great extent the compendium theologiae or textbook of the Middle Ages'); CE 'Doctors of the Church'

catholic.text: 3 September, a memorial in today's General Roman Calendar ('Saint Gregory the Great, Pope and Doctor of the Church'). Before 1969 it was 12 March, the day of his death, and the 1916 Roman Martyrology keeps 12 March. The 1916 Martyrology also marks 3 September as the day he was raised to the papacy.
catholic.source: USCCB readings, 3 September 2026 ('Memorial of Saint Gregory the Great, Pope and Doctor of the Church'); Roman Martyrology (1916), 12 March ('At Rome, St Gregory, pope and eminent doctor of the Church ... surnamed the Great, and called the Apostle of England') and 3 September ('the raising to the Sovereign Pontificate of St. Gregory the Great, an incomparable man'); Calendarium Romanum (1969)
catholic.note: The Martyrology copy is OCR ('Chnrch', 'snrnamed'); 'exact' keeps the OCR. Copy: archive.org/details/romanmartyrology00cathuoft (same file as the Martin and Ambrose research). The current (2004) Martyrology was not checked.

orthodox.text: 12 March in the Orthodox calendar: OCA ('Commemorated on March 12'), the Greek synaxarion (saint.gr: 'Εορτάζει στις 12 Μαρτίου'), and the Russian Church, whose old calendar puts 12 March on 25 March of the civil calendar (azbyka.ru: '25 марта'; orthodox.net: 'Commemorated March 12 (Civil Date: March 25 )').
orthodox.source: OCA, 'Saint Gregory Dialogus, Pope of Rome'; saint.gr 3826; azbyka.ru 'Григорий Двоеслов, Великий'; orthodox.net Menaion, 12 March
orthodox.note: Unlike Martin, every Orthodox source checked agrees on 12 March. GOARCH was not checked (403, as for Martin and Augustine). The Russian Church's 25 March civil date is the same day, 12 March, on the old calendar.

old_calendar_note.text: Churches on the old (Julian) calendar keep 12 March thirteen days later on today's calendar: 25 March.
old_calendar_note.note: The 13-day gap holds from 1900 to 2099. Checked directly for this date.

anglican.text: Church of England: 3 September, a Lesser Festival ('Gregory the Great, Bishop of Rome, Teacher of the Faith, 604'). The Episcopal Church (USA) keeps 12 March ('Gregory the Great, Bishop and Theologian, 604').
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar; The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar and pp. 131-133
anglican.note: Lesser Festival: on the CofE page the line is in roman type, not the italic used for Commemorations (checked in the page's HTML: no <em> tags on this line). LFF 2022: 'Gregory died on March 12, 604, and was buried in Saint Peter's'. So the two Anglican churches differ: England follows the Roman 3 September, the Episcopal Church keeps the old 12 March.

lutheran.text: The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod keeps 3 September ('Gregory the Great, Pastor'). The ELCA keeps 12 March ('Gregory the Great, Bishop of Rome, 604').
lutheran.source: LCMS, 'Commemorations' page (September: '3 - Gregory the Great, Pastor'); CPH blog, 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations' ('3 Gregory the Great, Pastor'); Evangelical Lutheran Worship, final draft January 2006, church year calendar (March: '12 Gregory the Great, Bishop of Rome, 604')
lutheran.note: Correction to the brief's expectation: the LCMS does NOT keep 12 March. The ELCA line is from the January 2006 final draft of ELW (Wayback copy), not the printed book, as for Martin, Augustine and Ambrose. CPH URL: https://blog.cph.org/read/church-year/commemorations .

why_dates_differ.text: 12 March is the day he died and was buried. Rome kept it from the 8th century. But it always falls in Lent, when saints' memorials are not kept, so the 1969 Roman calendar moved him to 3 September, the day he was made bishop of Rome in 590. The Orthodox, the Episcopal Church and the ELCA kept 12 March; the Church of England and the LCMS followed Rome's 3 September.
why_dates_differ.source: Calendarium Romanum (Vatican, 1969), commentary for 3 September: 'Festum S. Gregorii Magni inde a saeculo viii Romae semper celebratum est die eius depositionis, i. e. die 12 martii (604). Cum autem haec dies semper incidat in Quadragesima, memoria S. Gregorii in diem 3 septembris reponitur, qua die episcopus ordinatus est anno 590.'
why_dates_differ.note: Our translation: 'The feast of St Gregory the Great was always kept in Rome from the 8th century on the day of his burial, 12 March (604). But since this day always falls in Lent, the memorial of St Gregory is moved to 3 September, the day he was ordained bishop in 590.' The same book's general notes say memorials cannot be kept in Lent. Britannica: 'Western feast day, September 3 [formerly March 12, still observed in the East]'.

numbers.text: Thirteen years, six months and ten days as pope, says Bede.
numbers.quote: thirteen years, six months, and ten days
numbers.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 ('thirteen years, six months, and ten days'); the Whitby Life, chapter 32, gives the same

numbers.text: Monasteries he founded with his own money: six in Sicily and a seventh, St Andrew's, in his house in Rome.
numbers.quote: established six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh within the Roman walls
numbers.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1

numbers.text: English people baptised by Augustine at Christmas 597, as Gregory told his friend Eulogius.
numbers.quote: more than ten thousand Angli are reported to have been baptized
numbers.source: Gregory, Letters, Book 8, letter 30, to Eulogius of Alexandria
numbers.note: Gregory says 'at the solemnity of the Lord's Nativity which occurred in this first indiction': the first indiction ran from September 597, so Christmas 597. He says 'are reported'.

numbers.text: Monks in Augustine's party when they landed in Kent in 597.
numbers.quote: being, as is reported, nearly forty men
numbers.source: Bede, Book 1, chapter 25 ('being, as is reported, nearly forty men')

numbers.text: Nuns in Rome on the official list, for whom he bought bedding against the winter.
numbers.quote: they are found to be three thousand in number

numbers.text: People who fell dead in one hour during his plague procession in 590, as a deacon of Tours saw.
numbers.quote: in the space of one hour while the people uttered cries of supplication to the Lord eighty fell to the ground and died
numbers.source: Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1; Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 3, chapter 24
numbers.note: Grim, but it is the most-told fact of his election. Use only if the tone fits.

numbers.text: Books in his Moralia on Job.
numbers.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 ('in five and thirty books of exposition'); CE ('Moralium Libri XXXV')

numbers.text: Letters that survive, by the OCA's count.
numbers.source: OCA life ('His letters (848) ... have also survived')
numbers.note: Only the OCA gives a figure. Barmby's edition has 14 books of letters. If a second source is wanted, write 'about 850' or leave this number out.

traits.text: He loved quiet and felt the busy life was forced on him. He compared himself to Jacob, who loved Rachel but was given Leah first.
traits.title: homesick for quiet
traits.quote_exact: I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel, barren, but keen of sight and fair
traits.quote_display: I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel, barren, but keen of sight and fair
traits.source: Letters, Book 1, letter 5, to Theoctista, the emperor's sister (590); Dialogues, Book 1, preface
traits.note: Also Letter 1.5: 'For I have lost the deep joys of my quiet, and seem to have risen outwardly while inwardly falling down.' And Dialogues 1, preface: he went to 'a solitary place, very fit for a sad and melancholy disposition'. The personality test's Deep Well card uses both.

traits.text: He was often ill: stomach pains and slow fevers from youth, then gout. For his last years he was mostly in bed.
traits.title: ill for most of his life
traits.quote_exact: it is now almost full two years that I have been confined to my bed, afflicted with such pains of gout that I have hardly been able to rise on feast-days for as much as three hours space to solemnize mass.
traits.quote_display: it is now almost full two years that I have been confined to my bed, afflicted with such pains of gout that I have hardly been able to rise on feast-days for as much as three hours space to solemnize mass.
traits.source: Moralia, letter to Leander, section 5; Letters, Book 9, letter 123; Book 10, letter 35; Bede, Book 2, chapter 1
traits.note: Gregory of Tours blames his fasting: 'his stomach was weakened and he could scarcely stand upright'. Moralia letter to Leander: 'For many a year's circuit has gone by since I have been afflicted with frequent pains in the bowels'.

traits.text: He would not take grand titles. When Eulogius of Alexandria called him 'Universal Pope', he told him to stop.
traits.title: allergic to grand titles
traits.quote_exact: Away with words that inflate vanity and wound charity.
traits.quote_display: Away with words that inflate vanity and wound charity.
traits.source: Letters, Book 8, letter 30, to Eulogius; Book 7, letter 33, to the emperor Maurice
traits.note: Same letter: 'For my honour is the honour of the universal Church: my honour is the solid vigour of my brethren.' He called himself 'servant of the servants of God'.

traits.text: He was patient for a long time, then would not move. And he could be dry and cutting, even with the emperor.
traits.title: patient until pushed
traits.quote_exact: thou art well acquainted with my ways, that I bear long; but if once I have determined not to bear, I go gladly in the face of all dangers.
traits.quote_display: thou art well acquainted with my ways, that I bear long; but if once I have determined not to bear, I go gladly in the face of all dangers.
traits.source: Letters, Book 4, letter 47, to the deacon Sabinianus; Book 5, letter 40, to the emperor Maurice
traits.note: When Maurice called him simple (Book 5, letter 40): 'For by the use therein of the term simplicity they politely call me silly.'

traits.text: Strict, then tender. He had a dying monk who hid three gold coins shunned and buried in a dung heap. Thirty days later he pitied him and had Mass said for him for thirty days.
traits.title: severe, then sorry
traits.quote_exact: Thirty days after his departure, I began to take compassion upon him
traits.quote_display: Thirty days after his departure, I began to take compassion upon him
traits.note: He tells it himself. The monk, Justus, had nursed him: 'whiles I remained in the Abbey, served me very diligently, attending upon me in my often infirmities and sickness'.

traits.text: Generous to the poor, and on a large scale. He fed Rome from the Church's estates, and sent beds and cloaks as far as Mount Sinai.
traits.title: open-handed
traits.quote_exact: Other popes applied themselves to building churches or adorning them with gold and silver, but Gregory was wholly intent upon gaining souls.
traits.quote_display: Other popes applied themselves to building churches or adorning them with gold and silver, but Gregory was wholly intent upon gaining souls.
traits.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1; the epitaph in Bede; Letters, Book 11, letter 1 (to John, abbot of Mount Sinai: 'we have sent 15 cloaks, 30 rachanæ, and 15 beds'); CE on the grain doles
traits.note: Epitaph (Sellar's prose): 'Hunger and cold he overcame with food and raiment'. Britannica: 'his biographers record that he left the papal treasury nearly bankrupt'. Barmby's footnote thinks the Sinai abbot John was 'No doubt the John called Climacus': a guess, mark it as one.

others_on_him.text: A contemporary: Gregory of Tours heard of his election from his own deacon, who was in Rome and saw it.
others_on_him.who: Gregory of Tours, bishop and historian (died about 594)
others_on_him.quote: And such was his abstinence in food, his sleeplessness in prayer, his determination in fasting that his stomach was weakened and he could scarcely stand upright.
others_on_him.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1 (Brehaut, 1916)
others_on_him.note: Also: 'He was so versed in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric that he was believed second to none in the city.' The deacon 'saw his ordination with his own eyes'.

others_on_him.text: Bede, writing about 731, a century later, in the English church Gregory founded.
others_on_him.quote: for we may rightly, nay, we must, call him our apostle
others_on_him.note: And: 'Other popes applied themselves to building churches or adorning them with gold and silver, but Gregory was wholly intent upon gaining souls.'

others_on_him.text: His epitaph, as Bede copied it from the tomb.
others_on_him.who: The epitaph on his tomb at St Peter's
others_on_him.quote: Hunger and cold he overcame with food and raiment
others_on_him.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 (Sellar's prose rendering of the Latin verse)
others_on_him.note: It ends 'So, Consul of God, rejoice in this thy triumph'. Dudden (vol. 2, p. 269) says it was composed by Peter Oldradus, archbishop of Milan; not checked further.

others_on_him.text: Paul the Deacon, the historian of the Lombards (about 790), on his letter refusing to kill Lombards.
others_on_him.who: Paul the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino (died about 799)
others_on_him.quote: how humble this man was and of how great innocence and holiness
others_on_him.source: Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4, chapter 29 (Foulke, 1907)

others_on_him.text: John Calvin, a Protestant reformer, in 1559.
others_on_him.quote: Gregory, whom you may with justice call the last Bishop of Rome
others_on_him.source: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 4, chapter 17, section 49 (Henry Beveridge, 1845)
others_on_him.note: Calvin also attacks him (Book 3, chapter 24, section 9): 'Gregory, therefore, is most grievously and perniciously in error' (on assurance of election). Good for showing Protestant respect and dissent in one person.

life_moments.text: He was prefect of Rome, the city's highest civil office, by about 573. Gregory of Tours says he had worn silk and jewels. About a year later he gave it all up. He sold his goods for the poor, founded six monasteries on his Sicilian estates, and made his family house on the Caelian Hill into St Andrew's monastery. As pope he looked back on those years with longing. He also admitted he had been slow to go: 'for late and long I declined the grace of conversion'.
life_moments.title: The prefect becomes a monk
life_moments.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1; CE; Moralia, letter to Leander, section 1
life_moments.note: CE: 'a period to which he often refers as the happiest portion of his life' (CE's summary, not his words). His own: Dialogues 1, preface, remembers 'when I lived in mine Abbey'. Gregory of Tours: 'he sold the rest and all the furniture of his house and distributed the money among the poor in the city'.

life_moments.text: He was made a deacon (in 578, says the CE, before Pelagius II was pope), and Pope Pelagius II sent him to the emperor's court in Constantinople. Some of his monks went with him. With them he gave the talks on Job that became the Moralia, and he met Leander of Seville. He argued with the patriarch Eutychius, who taught that risen bodies would be 'impalpable, and more subtle than the wind and air'. Gregory pointed to the risen Christ: 'Handle Me and see'. The emperor took his side.
life_moments.title: Envoy in Constantinople
life_moments.source: CE; Bede, Book 2, chapter 1; Moralia, Book 14, sections 72-74
life_moments.note: The emperor's ruling and Eutychius's burned book are CE's account. Gregory stood godfather to the emperor Maurice's son: Gregory of Tours, 'whose son he had taken from the holy font'.

life_moments.text: The story goes that he saw boys for sale in the market in Rome, fair of skin and with beautiful hair. Told they were Angles, he said they had angels' faces. He asked the pope to let him go to Britain himself, and set out. The people of Rome made the pope call him back.
life_moments.title: The Angles in the market
life_moments.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 (a story 'handed down to us by the tradition of our ancestors'); Whitby Life, chapters 9-10 (Almond)
life_moments.note: Told as English tradition, not from Gregory's own writings. The Whitby Life (the oldest, c. 704-714) has visitors, not slaves, and his reply 'Angels of God'; Bede first makes them boys for sale (CE: 'It is Venerable Bede ... who first makes them slaves'). The Whitby Life adds that a locust landed on his book: 'stay in the place (Sta in loco)'. See misquoted_or_legend for 'Not Angles but angels'.

life_moments.text: In 589 the Tiber flooded and plague followed. Pope Pelagius died in February 590, and Rome chose Gregory. He wrote to the emperor asking him to refuse, but the city prefect stopped the letter. He led Rome in processions of prayer through the plague. A deacon of Tours who was there said eighty people fell dead in one hour as they prayed. When he got ready to hide, he was seized and carried to St Peter's, and made pope on 3 September 590.
life_moments.title: Carried to St Peter's
life_moments.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1; Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 3, chapter 24; Dudden vol. 1, p. 222 (date)
life_moments.note: Exact (Brehaut): 'And when Gregory was making ready to go to a hiding place he was seized and brought by force to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and there he was consecrated to the duties of bishop and made pope of the city.' Gregory of Tours: 'He strove earnestly to avoid this high office for fear that a certain pride at attaining the honor might sweep him back into the worldly vanities he had rejected.' The later tale of three days in the woods and a pillar of light is legend (see misquoted_or_legend).

life_moments.text: As soon as he was pope he wrote the Pastoral Rule, a book on how a bishop should live and how to speak to each kind of person. He dedicated it to John of Ravenna. It became the handbook of bishops for centuries. It ends with him asking his reader's prayers: he has been like an ugly painter painting a handsome man.
life_moments.title: A book for pastors
life_moments.source: Pastoral Rule, Part 1, chapter 1 and Part 4; CE ('At the very outset of his pontificate'; 'it remained for centuries the textbook of the Catholic episcopate')
life_moments.note: Exact (Barmby, Part 4): 'I have been as an ill-favoured painter pourtraying a handsome man'. The Christian Personality Test is built on Book 3 of this work. Year: CE says 'At the very outset'; '591' is a common modern date, not checked in a source. Safer: 'In his first year as pope'.

life_moments.text: The Lombards took Italian towns and came up to Rome's walls, and help from the emperor was slow. Gregory paid ransoms, fed refugees, appointed a commander on his own authority and bargained for peace, often against the emperor's wishes. He refused to have a hand in killing even the invaders.
life_moments.title: Rome's defender
life_moments.source: Letters, Book 4, letter 47; Britannica ('twice preventing Rome from being sacked by the Lombards'); CE ('appointing a tribune on his own authority'; peace 'signed in 599'); Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4
life_moments.note: Exact (Barmby, 4.47): 'But, since I fear God, I shrink from having anything to do with the death of any one.' Britannica: the Lombards' 'swords were held back only by daily ransom from the church'. Peace was signed in 599 (CE).

life_moments.text: He sent Augustine, a monk of his own monastery, with about forty monks to the English. On the way they lost their nerve and sent Augustine back to ask to come home. Gregory wrote them a letter telling them to go on. They landed in Kent. At Christmas 597, he heard, more than ten thousand English were baptised.
life_moments.title: The mission to the English
life_moments.source: Bede, Book 1, chapters 23 and 25; Letters, Book 8, letter 30, to Eulogius
life_moments.note: Gregory's letter (in Bede 1.23): 'though I cannot labour with you, I shall partake in the joy of the reward, because I am willing to labour'. Bede: they 'were seized with craven terror, and began to think of returning home'. Gregory calls Augustine 'a monk of my monastery' (Letter 8.30); his letter in Bede makes him their abbot ('When Augustine, your Superior, returns, whom we also constitute your abbot'). Later sources call him prior of St Andrew's: not checked.

life_moments.text: He sent word to Augustine, through Abbot Mellitus, not to tear down the English temples but to smash the idols and make the temples churches. The people could keep their feast days in a changed form. People climb, he said, by steps, not leaps. And when he heard of miracles in England, he warned Augustine not to let them make him proud.
life_moments.title: Steps, not leaps
life_moments.source: Letters, Book 11, letter 76, to Mellitus (in Bede, Book 1, chapter 30); Book 11, letter 28, to Augustine
life_moments.note: Exact (Barmby, 11.76): 'since one who strives to ascend to the highest place must needs rise by steps or paces, and not by leaps.' Exact (11.28): 'rejoice, that is, because the souls of the Angli are drawn by outward miracles to inward grace; but tremble, lest among the signs that are done the infirm mind lift itself up to presumption about itself'. He had earlier (11.66) told King Ethelbert to 'overturn the edifices of their temples'; the Mellitus letter changes course. Say so plainly.

life_moments.text: His last years were spent mostly in bed with gout. In 603 he welcomed the new emperor Phocas, who had murdered Maurice and his sons, with a warm letter. In December 603 he wrote to the Lombard queen Theodelinda that he could hardly rise, 'not only for dictating, but even for speaking'. He died on 12 March 604.
life_moments.title: The last years
life_moments.source: Letters, Book 13, letter 31; Book 14, letter 12; Foulke's note to History of the Lombards, Book 4 ('Pope Gregory in Dec., 603, had written to Theudelinda'); Dudden vol. 2, p. 268

summary.text: Gregory's own contemporaries record no miracles by him. Gregory of Tours tells of his election with no wonders. The stories come later: from a monk of Whitby in England (about 704-714), from Paul the Deacon (about 770-780, in a section scholars think was added later), and from John the Deacon in Rome (873-875). The Whitby writer says himself that he had only common report. Gregory's own Dialogues are full of other people's miracles, and he tells of wonders in his own monastery (Justus, Book 4, chapter 55; Eleutherius, Book 3, chapter 33).
summary.source: Gasquet's Whitby Life (1904), introduction (the Whitby Life is 'the source and first authority for the most notable miraculous occurrences reported of St. Gregory'); Almond (1904); Dudden vol. 2, pp. 269-272; CE ('The miracles attributed to Gregory are very many')
summary.note: Keep the section, but frame it as 'what later writers told of him', each with its date. Martin's model: tell as the source tells it, then 'Doubted from the start' in the sources' own words. Unlike Martin's Sulpicius, no eyewitness wrote these down.

his_own_view.text: Gregory himself put character above miracles.
his_own_view.quote: For true judgment of one's life is to be taken from his virtuous conversation, and not from the working of miracles
his_own_view.note: Also Dialogues 1.2, on Libertinus: 'the patience of so worthy a man did far excel all his signs and miracles'. The Whitby Life (chapter 4) quotes a line of Gregory's to the same effect.

items.text: A Roman lady who baked the bread for Mass smiled when Gregory gave it to her as the Body of Christ. She had made that bread with her own hands, she said. Gregory had the people pray. On the altar the bread was found as a bleeding piece like the tip of a little finger. She saw it and believed. At their prayer it became bread again, and she received it.
items.title: The bread that bled
items.witness: None named. The Whitby writer calls it 'a story of the old ones' ('antiquorum fertur esse narratio').
items.quote_en: a bloodied small piece of a little finger (our translation)
items.source: Whitby Life, chapter 20 (Gasquet's Latin, 1904, pp. 24-26); also in Paul the Deacon's Life and John the Deacon's (Dudden vol. 2, p. 272)
items.note: Her words: 'Ego ipsos panes meis feci manibus' ('I made these very loaves with my own hands', our translation). Dudden (vol. 2, pp. 271-272) calls it 'the legend of the mass of Gregory'. The late-medieval pictures of the 'Mass of St Gregory' show Christ appearing; the early story has no vision of Christ, only the bread.

items.text: Someone of his household, the Whitby writer heard, saw a white dove sitting on him while he composed his homilies on Ezekiel. Gregory was angry and forbade him to tell anyone while he lived. A later, fuller version: his secretary Peter made a hole in the curtain between them and saw a dove whiter than snow with its beak at Gregory's lips; when it drew back, Gregory spoke and Peter wrote.
items.when: Told about 704-714; the fuller version later
items.title: The dove at his lips
items.witness: 'A certain one of his household' (Whitby); Peter the Deacon (Paul the Deacon's Life, told after Gregory's death)
items.quote_latin: albam sedisse columbam cum in predictum Ezechielem fecit omelias
items.quote_en: that a white dove sat on him while he was composing the homilies on Ezekiel (our translation)
items.source: Whitby Life, chapter 26 (Gasquet's Latin); Paul the Deacon, Life of Gregory, chapter 28 (PL 75); CE ('A dove is his special emblem, in allusion to the well-known story')
items.note: Paul's Latin (PL 75 OCR): 'vidit columbam nive candidiorem super ejuscnput sedentem' ('saw a dove whiter than snow sitting on his head'). Dudden (vol. 2, p. 269, note 2): 'This chapter, however, occurs among the interpolations in Paul's biography.' CE wrongly credits the story to 'Peter the Deacon (Vita, xxviii)': the Vita is Paul's; Peter is the witness in it.

items.text: Passing through Trajan's Forum, Gregory remembered a story of the pagan emperor Trajan: he stopped on the way to war to give justice to a widow. Gregory went to St Peter's and wept for Trajan's soul until he was told his prayer was heard. He was also told never to ask it again for a pagan.
items.title: Tears for Trajan
items.witness: None. The Whitby writer: 'some of ours say it was told by the Romans'.
items.quote_latin: quidam quoque de nostris dicunt narratum a Romanis
items.quote_en: some of our people say it was told by the Romans (our translation)
items.source: Whitby Life, chapter 29 (Gasquet's Latin); Paul the Deacon, Life, chapter 27 (PL 75); Dudden vol. 2, p. 271
items.note: Gasquet (1904): the story was 'harder to swallow in those days even than in these'. He notes the English writer blames the Romans for it, while the Roman John the Deacon says it is read in the English churches. Dante later used it (not checked here).

items.text: Gregory tells this one himself. A monk-doctor of his monastery, Justus, died after hiding three gold coins. Thirty days later Gregory had Mass offered for him every day for thirty days. On the thirtieth day, the dead monk appeared to his brother Copiosus and said he was now well, 'for this day have I received the communion'.
items.title: The thirtieth Mass
items.witness: Copiosus, the monk's brother, 'who yet liveth' when Gregory wrote; the monks, who counted the days
items.quote: Hitherto have I been in bad case, but now I am well; for this day have I received the communion
items.note: The origin of the 'Gregorian Masses' (thirty Masses for the dead) is a later custom; not checked in a source here, so do not claim it.

items.text: When chosen pope, the Whitby Life says, he had himself carried out of Rome hidden in a basket by merchants and hid in the woods for three days. A pillar of light over the forest showed the people where he was.
items.title: The pillar of light
items.quote_en: a most bright pillar entered the wood (our translation)
items.source: Whitby Life, chapter 7 (Gasquet's Latin); Paul the Deacon, Life, chapter 13, and John the Deacon, Life, Book 1, chapter 44 (per Dudden vol. 1, p. 221, note 3: 'Both Paul and John got the story from the S. Gallen Life, 7')
items.note: Contradicted by the eyewitness account in Gregory of Tours (he was seized before he could hide). CE: 'seems to be pure invention'. The Orthodox Prologue of Ohrid still tells it. Put it in misquoted_or_legend or in 'Doubted from the start', not as a miracle told straight.

items.text: A relic story Gregory told of an earlier pope, Leo: when Greeks doubted that cloths laid on martyrs' tombs were true relics, Leo cut one with scissors and blood flowed. The Whitby Life later tells a similar story of Gregory himself.
items.when: Gregory's letter to the empress Constantina
items.title: The cloth that bled
items.witness: Gregory: 'as has been handed down from our forefathers'
items.quote: the aforesaid pontiff took scissors and cut this same cloth (brandeum), and from the very incision blood flowed
items.source: Letters, Book 4, letter 30, to the empress Constantina (Barmby); Whitby Life, chapter 21; Dudden vol. 2, pp. 271-272 ('related by Gregory of Pope Leo, and was afterwards transferred by his biographer to Gregory himself')
items.note: A good example of how a story moved from one pope to another. Optional.

doubt.text: The Whitby writer on his own sources.
doubt.quote: we have only common report; we have not learnt orally from those who saw or heard;
doubt.source: T. Leo Almond, 'The Whitby Life of St. Gregory', Downside Review 23 (1904), introduction (Almond's rendering of the author's words)
doubt.note: The Latin (chapter 30, Gasquet): '... quae etiam non ab illis qui viderunt et audierunt per ore didicimus, vulgata tantum habemus'. In chapter 3 he says he writes though 'cum pauca eius de gestis audivimus signorum' ('we have heard few of his deeds of wonder', our translation). In chapter 30 he even asks readers not to be troubled if some of these stories were really about another saint.

doubt.text: On Gregory's death the same writer says:
doubt.quote: Of the death of this man, how and of what manner it was, we have not heard.

doubt.text: A modern historian's judgement on the dove and the later tales.
doubt.quote: are not sufficiently well attested to be accepted as sober history
doubt.source: F. Homes Dudden, Gregory the Great (1905), vol. 2, p. 270
doubt.note: Full sentence: 'The details of these stories, which have been repeated with more or less fidelity by later writers, are not sufficiently well attested to be accepted as sober history.'

misquoted_or_legend.text: 'Not Angles but angels' (Non Angli sed angeli).
misquoted_or_legend.said: Gregory saw English slave boys in Rome and said, 'Not Angles, but angels.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The neat Latin line is in neither early source. Bede (about 731) has him say 'for they have an angelic face, and it is meet that such should be co-heirs with the Angels in heaven', and says the story came 'by the tradition of our ancestors'. The older Whitby Life has him answer 'Angels of God', and has the Angles as visitors, not slaves. Gregory's own writings never tell the story.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 (Sellar); Whitby Life, chapter 9 (Almond); CE
misquoted_or_legend.note: CE: 'The first mention of the event is in the Whitby life (c, ix), and the whole story seems to be an English tradition.' Foulke's 1907 footnote repeats 'not Angles but angels' as fact: an example of the misquote. Where the crisp form first appears was not traced.

misquoted_or_legend.said: Gregory wrote or collected the chant named after him.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The chant is named after him, but nothing in his own writings, his epitaph, the Whitby Life, Paul the Deacon or Bede connects him with it. The claim appears in the 8th and 9th centuries. Dudden (1905): 'the weight of evidence makes against the truth of the tradition'. Britannica still gives the tradition ('According to tradition, Pope Gregory I codified and organized ...') and adds that the chant took its surviving form in the Frankish lands in the 8th and 9th centuries.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Dudden vol. 1, pp. 271-273; CE ('the earliest authority seems to be John the Deacon'); Britannica, 'Gregorian chant'
misquoted_or_legend.note: Be fair: say 'tradition credits him; historians doubt he had a hand in it'. Dudden: 'It is now generally believed by musical experts that Gregory had nothing whatever to do either with the compilation of the Antiphonary' (the sentence runs across a page break).

misquoted_or_legend.text: Gregory invented the seven deadly sins.
misquoted_or_legend.said: Gregory drew up the list of the seven deadly sins: pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: His list is different. Pride is not one of the seven but 'the root of all evil', the queen who hands the heart to 'seven principal sins': 'vain glory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice, gluttony, lust'. Sloth is not on it; melancholy (sadness) is. The familiar list came later.
misquoted_or_legend.note: Britannica says he 'enumerated the seven deadly sins' in the Moralia: true in outline, but the list differs. Useful beside the site's deadly-sins quiz. The date of the later list was not checked; say only 'later'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: The Gregorian calendar is named after him.
misquoted_or_legend.said: Pope Gregory the Great gave us the Gregorian calendar.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: It is named for a different pope, Gregory XIII, 'who issued the papal bull Inter gravissimas in 1582'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: He hid in the woods and a pillar of light gave him away.
misquoted_or_legend.said: Chosen pope, Gregory fled Rome hidden in a basket and hid in a forest for three days, until a pillar of fire showed where he was.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Gregory of Tours, whose own deacon was in Rome, says he was seized while 'making ready to go to a hiding place'. CE: 'The story that Gregory actually fled the city and remained hidden in a forest for three days, when his whereabouts was revealed by a supernatural light, seems to be pure invention.'
misquoted_or_legend.source: Whitby Life, chapter 7 (Gasquet's Latin); Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1; CE
misquoted_or_legend.note: The Prologue of Ohrid (1985 English, copyright) still tells the 'fiery column'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: St Michael sheathed his sword over Castel Sant'Angelo and ended the plague.
misquoted_or_legend.said: During Gregory's plague procession the Archangel Michael appeared on Hadrian's tomb, sheathing his sword, and the plague stopped.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The eyewitness account (Gregory of Tours) has the procession but no angel. CE calls the angel 'the legend'; Britannica says 'According to tradition'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: CE; Britannica; Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1
misquoted_or_legend.note: Britannica adds that the Seven Penitential Psalms tied to this procession 'date from the 12th century and have been incorrectly ascribed to Gregory'. The first written source of the angel story was not traced.

misquoted_or_legend.text: He burned the Palatine library to stamp out the classics.
misquoted_or_legend.said: Gregory the Great burned the imperial library on the Palatine and banned Livy.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Gibbon, no friend of popes, reports the story and doubts it: 'But the evidence of his destructive rage is doubtful and recent'. His note traces it to John of Salisbury and two others: 'the oldest of the three lived in the xiith century'. What is true: Gregory scolded a bishop for teaching the pagan poets (Letters, Book 11, letter 54).
misquoted_or_legend.source: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 45, with note 62
misquoted_or_legend.note: Gibbon: 'It is commonly believed, that Pope Gregory the First attacked the temples and mutilated the statues of the city; that, by the command of the Barbarian, the Palatine library was reduced to ashes'. John of Salisbury's own text was not fetched.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Calvin called him 'the last good pope'.
misquoted_or_legend.said: John Calvin called Gregory the Great 'the last good pope'.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: His words are 'Gregory, whom you may with justice call the last Bishop of Rome'. He meant the last true bishop before the papacy he rejected. Elsewhere he says Gregory 'is most grievously and perniciously in error' (Book 3, chapter 24, section 9).
misquoted_or_legend.note: That the 'last good pope' form is common online was not measured; keep this item only if the page wants it.

rows.line: For, when we administer necessaries of any kind to the indigent, we do not bestow our own, but render them what is theirs; we rather pay a debt of justice than accomplish works of mercy.

rows.statement: If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to.
rows.line: We should love those joined to us by kinship of the flesh, whom we know as our neighbours; but those we suffer as adversaries on the way of God we should refuse to know, by hating and fleeing them.
rows.note: Own translation: checked against the Latin, not a PD English text.

rows.statement: A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience.
rows.work_on_site: Letter to Gennadius, governor of Africa
rows.note: Hidden on the site (hide:true); not checked here.

rows.statement: Governments should use their laws to promote the Christian faith.
rows.work_on_site: Letter to King Æthelberht of Kent
rows.line: Make haste to extend the Christian faith among the peoples under your sway.
rows.place: Book 11, letter 66, to King Ethelbert of Kent
rows.note: CCEL (unrevised) reads 'under thy sway'. Bede copies the letter (Book 1, chapter 32).

rows.statement: In the end, God will save everyone.
rows.line: Certain it is, and without all doubt most true, that as the good shall have no end of their joys, so the wicked never any release of their torments.
rows.note: The sentence continues: 'for our Saviour himself ...'.

friends_family_rivals.text: A noblewoman who took religious vows after her husband died. Catholics keep her on 3 November; the OCA gives 4 November.
friends_family_rivals.source: CE ('She is honoured as a saint, her feast being kept on 3 November'); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 3 November ('St. Sylvia, mother of pope St. Gregory'); OCA ('his mother Sylvia (November 4)'); Britannica ('Silvia, took vows on the death of her husband')

friends_family_rivals.text: A rich Roman, perhaps a church official. He owned estates in Sicily and the house on the Caelian Hill.
friends_family_rivals.source: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1 ('son of Gordianus'); CE; Britannica ('held an office, possibly defensor')

friends_family_rivals.text: His father's sisters, who with a third sister gave their lives to prayer. Gregory tells how Tarsilla saw their ancestor Pope Felix in a vision before she died.
friends_family_rivals.source: Dialogues, Book 4, chapter 16 ('concerning mine aunt Tarsilla'; 'Felix, my great-grandfather, sometime Bishop of this see of Rome'); saint.gr; OCA
friends_family_rivals.note: Gardner's English says 'great-grandfather'; Britannica and Dudden say great-great-grandfather (the Latin 'atavus'). Say 'an ancestor'. The 1916 Martyrology keeps Felix III on 25 February as 'great-grandfather of St. Gregory the Great'.

friends_family_rivals.text: His deacon and secretary, whom he had loved since Peter was young. The Dialogues are written as talks with him.
friends_family_rivals.source: Dialogues, Book 1, preface ('Peter, my dear son and deacon ... a man whom, from his younger years, I had always loved most entirely'); Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4, chapter 5

friends_family_rivals.text: Gregory never met him. He wrote the only early life of Benedict (Dialogues, Book 2), from what four of Benedict's monks told him.
friends_family_rivals.rel: the monk whose life he wrote
friends_family_rivals.source: Dialogues, Book 2, preface ('I had by the relation of four of his disciples': Constantinus, Valentinianus, Simplicius, Honoratus)
friends_family_rivals.note: The site's pair line: 'Gregory the Great wrote the only early life of Benedict.' Benedict's death year (about 547) was not checked here.

friends_family_rivals.text: Bishop of Seville. They met in Constantinople and stayed friends. Gregory sent him the Moralia, and they wrote to each other about their gout.
friends_family_rivals.source: Moralia, letter to Leander; Letters, Book 9, letter 121 ('Your Holiness writes of being afflicted with the pains of gout, by continual suffering from which I too am grievously worn down.')

friends_family_rivals.text: A monk of Gregory's own monastery, sent to convert the English, and made their first bishop.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letters, Book 8, letter 30 ('a monk of my monastery'); Bede, Book 1, chapters 23-33, and Book 2, chapter 1 ('the holy Augustine, the first bishop of the English nation'); Letters, Book 11, letters 28 and 64

friends_family_rivals.text: Patriarch of Alexandria and a friend by letter. Gregory told him of the English baptisms, and scolded him for calling him 'Universal Pope'.
A Catholic queen married to the Lombard king Agilulf. Gregory sent her his Dialogues and worked through her for peace.
friends_family_rivals.source: Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4, chapters 5-6 ('The aforesaid pope then sent these books to queen Theudelinda'); Letters, Book 14, letter 12

friends_family_rivals.text: The emperor. Gregory stood godfather to his son, but they clashed over the Lombards and over church titles. In 595 Maurice sent him a letter, now lost, 'accusing him of being both a traitor and a fool' (CE). Gregory's reply: 'they politely call me silly'.
friends_family_rivals.rel: godfather to his son; sparring partner
friends_family_rivals.source: Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1 ('whose son he had taken from the holy font'); Letters, Book 5, letter 40; CE

friends_family_rivals.text: Patriarch of Constantinople, who used the title 'Ecumenical (universal) Patriarch'. Gregory called any such title proud and wrote to him and to the emperor about it.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letters, Book 5, letter 18; Book 7, letter 33 ('whosoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist'); Britannica

friends_family_rivals.text: Patriarch of Constantinople who taught that risen bodies cannot be touched. Gregory argued it out with him before the emperor.
friends_family_rivals.source: Moralia, Book 14, sections 72-74; Bede, Book 2, chapter 1; CE

friends_family_rivals.text: Bishop of Marseilles who smashed the pictures in his churches because people worshipped them. Gregory praised his zeal and blamed his breaking them.
The usurping emperor who killed Maurice and his sons. Gregory greeted him warmly.
A monk of Mount Sinai to whom Gregory sent beds and cloaks for an old people's home, asking his prayers. Barmby thought him John Climacus, author of The Ladder.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letters, Book 11, letter 1; Barmby's footnote 123 ('No doubt the John called Climacus')
friends_family_rivals.note: The identification is Barmby's guess. Mark it 'perhaps'.

how_he_died.big: He died in Rome on 12 March 604, after years of gout, and was buried the same day at St Peter's.
paras: From about 599 he was mostly in bed. He wrote that he could hardly rise on feast days to say Mass.
His letters speak of pain and of wanting to die: 'every day I faint under my sufferings, and sigh in expectation of the relief of death'.
In December 603 he wrote to Queen Theodelinda that the gout left him hardly able to speak. Her envoys left him 'in the utmost peril and danger of our life'.
No last words were recorded. The Whitby monk wrote that he had not heard how Gregory died.
details_exact: it is now eleven months since it has been a very rare case with me if I have been able now and then to rise from my bed
For every day I faint under my sufferings, and sigh in expectation of the relief of death.
But so great an infirmity from gout has held us fast as to render us hardly able to rise, not only for dictating, but even for speaking
found us weak, and when they departed, left us in the utmost peril and danger of our life
Of the death of this man, how and of what manner it was, we have not heard.
how_he_died.sources: Letters, Book 9, letter 123 (599, per Dudden vol. 2, pp. 38-39); Book 10, letter 35; Book 14, letter 12 (December 603, per Foulke); Whitby Life, chapter 32 (Almond); Dudden vol. 2, p. 268; Bede, Book 2, chapter 1

later.text: After his death came famine, and his successor Sabinian stopped Gregory's free grain. Paul the Deacon's Life says Gregory appeared to him three times in a vision to rebuke him, and the fourth time struck him on the head, and he soon died.
later.source: Paul the Deacon, Life of Gregory, chapter 29 (PL 75); Dudden vol. 2, pp. 269-270
later.note: A later story (8th century). Dudden: 'not sufficiently well attested to be accepted as sober history'.

later.text: John the Deacon (873-875) says a mob wanted to burn Gregory's books, and Peter the Deacon saved them by swearing on the Gospels that he had seen the dove, then died as he finished speaking.
later.source: John the Deacon, Life, Book 4, chapter 69 (as summarised by Dudden vol. 2, p. 270)
later.note: Latin not checked; Dudden's summary only.

how_he_died.note: Dudden (vol. 2, p. 268): 'His release came on the 12th of March, 604, and on the same day he was buried in the portico of the Basilica of St. Peter, in front of the sacristy.' Britannica: 'his biographers record that he left the papal treasury nearly bankrupt'.

is_he_a_saint.big: Yes, in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Lutherans keep his day. He was hailed as a saint as soon as he died.

churches.status: Saint and Doctor of the Church
churches.note: One of the four great Latin Doctors (with Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome). Memorial on 3 September.
churches.source: USCCB; CE 'Doctors of the Church' (Boniface VIII's decree of 1298)

churches.note: Gregory the Dialogist, 12 March. The Orthodox credit him with the Lenten Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts.
Church of England Lesser Festival, 3 September ('Teacher of the Faith'); Episcopal Church, 12 March.

how.text: No formal canonization: CE says he was acclaimed a saint by the people at once.
how.source: CE ('His canonization by popular acclamation followed at once on his death, and survived a reaction against his memory which seems to have occurred soon afterwards')

orthodox_note.text: The Orthodox honour him although he was a pope, and credit him with the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, used on weekdays in Lent.
orthodox_note.source: OCA ('Saint Gregory compiled the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts in the Latin language, which before him was known only in the verbal tradition'); azbyka.ru; orthochristian.com
orthodox_note.note: This is the Orthodox tradition as the OCA states it. Many scholars doubt the attribution; no source for that view was fetched (could_not_verify). Print it as 'the Orthodox credit him with', not as fact.

protestant_note.text: Calvin respected him but attacked some of his teaching.

main.exact: And dispose our days in thy peace, and bid us to be preserved from eternal damnation, and to be numbered in the flock of thine elect.
main.display: And dispose our days in Thy peace, and bid us to be preserved from eternal damnation, and to be numbered in the flock of Thine elect.
main.latin: Diesque nostros in tua pace disponas, atque ab aeterna damnatione nos eripi, et in electorum tuorum iubeas grege numerari.
main.work: Words he added to the prayer of the Mass, as Bede reports
main.source: A. M. Sellar (tr.), 1907; Latin from The Latin Library
main.note: Bede: 'in the celebration of Masses, he added three petitions of the utmost perfection'. These words are still in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I); that last fact was not checked in a missal here. The Liber Pontificalis also reports it (not fetched).

prayer_he_wrote.none_other: No other prayer to God in his own works was found. The Pastoral Rule and the Moralia end with requests for the reader's prayers, which are not prayers to God. No prayer TO him is given.

He was also a monk and founded seven monasteries (Gregory of Tours; CE calls him 'the first monk-pope'), so 'monks' is defensible if the hub wants founders there. Flag for the main session.

personality_test.text: The Christian Personality Test names 'St Gregory the Great' among the saints of The Deep Well: 'The man whose book this test is built on.' This is the site's reading, not a church's.
personality_test.deepwell_card_text: The man whose book this test is built on. His Dialogues begin with him sitting alone in a quiet place. He says it suited 'a sad and melancholy disposition'. He also wrote that he loved the quiet life and had the busy one forced on him.
checks: I retired myself into a solitary place, very fit for a sad and melancholy disposition
I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel, barren, but keen of sight and fair
personality_test.note: Both lines check (Dialogues 1, preface; Letters 1.5). He is not in any OPPOSITES pair. The live URL was not opened. The whole test is built on his Pastoral Rule, Part 3, and the Moralia (see personality.json SPEAKER/credits).

hard_topics.text: In 602 the soldier Phocas overthrew the emperor Maurice and had him and his sons killed. In 603 Gregory wrote Phocas a joyful letter of welcome. Critics have called it a stain on him. Defenders say he may not have known how Phocas came to power, and that he honoured the office, not the man.
quotes: Glory to God in the highest who, according as it is written, changes times, and transfers kingdoms
who rejoice that the Benignity of your Piety has arrived at imperial supremacy
display: Glory to God in the highest Who, according as it is written, changes times, and transfers kingdoms
who rejoice that the Benignity of your Piety has arrived at imperial supremacy
critics: has sullied, with indelible disgrace, the character of the saint (Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 46)
addressed to the usurper a paean of praise and thanksgiving that has cast a stain upon the memory of this great pope (Foulke, 1907)
defenders: Every kind of judgement has been passed upon Gregory for writing these letters, but the question remains a difficult one. (CE)
But the judgment of his critics is perhaps too severe. (Foulke, 1907)
hard_topics.source: Letters, Book 13, letter 31 (Barmby); Gibbon chapter 46; CE; Foulke's note to History of the Lombards Book 3; Britannica ('his dislike of Maurice explains his warm welcome to Phocas, the bloody usurper')
hard_topics.note: CE's defence: 'his ignorance of the way in which Phocus [sic] had reached the throne' and 'his view that the emperor was God's representative on earth'.

hard_topics.text: He forbade forcing Jews into baptism and ordered synagogues wrongly taken to be paid for. He held that Jews should have no more than the law allowed, and no less. But he also offered lower rents to Jewish tenants who became Christians, and enforced the ban on Jews owning Christian slaves. Britannica: 'His concern with justice for Jews was limited.'
quotes: For, when any one is brought to the font of baptism, not by the sweetness of preaching, but by compulsion, he returns to his former superstition, and dies the worse from having been born again.
so neither damage nor any cost ought to be brought upon them contrary to justice and equity
if any of them should be willing to become Christians, some little of their dues be remitted to them, to the end that others also, incited by this benefit, may be moved to a like desire.
hard_topics.source: Letters, Book 1, letter 47; Book 9, letter 55; Book 2, letter 32 (Barmby); Britannica; CE
hard_topics.note: CE: 'It is curious, therefore, to find him acting as a champion and protector of the Jews.' The later papal bulls called 'Sicut Judaeis' took their opening from a letter of his: not checked, leave out.

hard_topics.text: Where persuasion failed he used pressure. He told a bishop in Sardinia to load pagan peasants on church land with such heavy dues that they would convert. His own 1895 translator called this an inconsistency.
quotes: he must be weighted with so great a burden of payment as to be compelled by the very pain of the exaction to hasten to the right way
critics: This is not the only instance of religious zeal betraying him into a certain human inconsistency. (Barmby, footnote to Book 4, letter 26)
Rural pagans fared worse: Ruthless measures forced them to abandon their cults, and Gregory advised Brunhild to use armed force against them. (Britannica)
hard_topics.source: Letters, Book 4, letter 26 (Barmby) and Barmby's note 1549; Britannica; CE ('if gentler treatment failed, he had no hesitation in accordance with the ideas of his age, in resorting to compulsion')

hard_topics.text: He freed some slaves of the Church, saying people were born free by nature. He also bought English boys in Gaul to be given to monasteries, and ran church estates in an age of slavery without calling for its end. Britannica: he 'did tolerate slavery'.
quotes: it is a salutary deed if men whom nature originally produced free, and whom the law of nations has subjected to the yoke of slavery, be restored by the benefit of manumission to the liberty in which they were born.
English boys of about seventeen or eighteen years of age, who may profit by being given to God in monasteries
hard_topics.source: Letters, Book 6, letter 12 (freeing Montana and Thomas); Book 6, letter 7, to Candidus; Britannica
hard_topics.note: The Candidus letter does not say the boys were slaves; Barmby's reading and later scholars take them as bought slave boys. Say 'bought', as the letter says 'procure'.

hard_topics.text: In a sermon he said that the sinful woman of Luke 7, Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene were one woman. The Catholic calendar of 1969 separated them again: its 22 July memorial is of Mary Magdalene only, 'to whom Christ first appeared after His resurrection'.
quotes_latin: Hanc vero quam Lucas peccatricem mulierem, Joannes Mariam nominat, illam esse Mariam credimus de qua Marcus septem daemonia ejecta fuisse testatur.
quotes_en: This woman whom Luke calls a sinful woman, John names Mary; we believe her to be the Mary from whom, Mark testifies, seven demons were cast out. (our translation)
hard_topics.source: Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 33 (PL 76; OCR reads 'Maiiam' and '7 Marcus'); Calendarium Romanum 1969, 22 July ('iam non habebitur memoria Mariae de Bethania neque mulieris peccatricis de qua agitur in Lc 7, 36-50, sed tantum de Maria Magdalena')
hard_topics.note: He does not use the word 'prostitute'; he calls her a sinner ('peccatrix'). The 1969 quote is our translation of 'sed tantum de Maria Magdalena cui Christus post suam resurrectionem primae apparuit'. How widely the West followed him was not checked in a source: do not say 'for centuries' without one.

hard_topics.text: He rebuked a bishop for teaching grammar with the pagan poets: the praises of Christ and of Jupiter cannot share one mouth. The later story that he burned the Palatine library is legend.
quotes: we changed what had been said before into groaning and sadness, since the praises of Christ cannot find room in one mouth with the praises of Jupiter.
hard_topics.source: Letters, Book 11, letter 54, to Desiderius of Vienne; Gibbon chapter 45

hard_topics.text: In the Dialogues he teaches a cleansing fire after death for small sins, and that the damned suffer for ever. The Reformers rejected purgatory: Calvin called it 'a deadly device of Satan'.
quotes: But yet we must believe that before the day of judgment there is a Purgatory fire for certain small sins
Certain it is, and without all doubt most true, that as the good shall have no end of their joys, so the wicked never any release of their torments
hard_topics.source: Dialogues, Book 4, chapters 39 and 44 (P.W./Gardner); Calvin, Institutes, Book 3, chapter 5, section 6 ('cry aloud that purgatory is a deadly device of Satan')
hard_topics.note: The Orthodox position on purgatory was not sourced here; leave it out rather than guess.

checker_2026_09_25.by: Adversarial checker, 25 Sep 2026, against the primary texts in sources/people/gregory-the-great/
fixes: Deacon: the CE says "in 578, the pope ordained him" deacon; Pelagius II became pope only in 579. Page now says "He was made a deacon, and Pope Pelagius II sent him as his envoy". Envoy role line now "about 579 to 586" (CE: spring 579; recalled 586 "or possibly 585").
Eutychius: Moralia 14 (and the CE) have a debate that ended in a PRIVATE audience with the emperor, who had the book burned. "Argued in public" removed; "and had the patriarch's book burned" added.

Angles: Bede (Sellar) has boys "of fair complexion, with pleasing countenances, and very beautiful hair", not "fair-haired". "Back in Rome" removed: Bede gives no date, the Whitby Life puts it under Pope Benedict I (574-578, before Constantinople), the CE puts it after 586.

Numbers: Bede's "nearly forty men" are the party that LANDED on Thanet (with Frankish interpreters picked up on the way), so the chip is "Landed in Kent", not "Sent to the English". Monasteries: the cited source (Gregory of Tours) says "a seventh within the Roman walls"; the line now says so.

Miracles lede: "No one of his own time records a miracle by him" is a universal negative no source here states; now "Gregory of Tours, writing in his lifetime, tells of his election with no wonders at all". Whitby date "between about 704 and 714" is not in any source (Almond: relics moved 675-704, not later than 713 if Elfleda was alive; CE: "probably about 713"): now "early in the 700s". "Gregory himself tells one wonder, from his own monastery" was wrong (Dialogues 3.33, Eleutherius, is another): now "tells of wonders in his own monastery, like the one below".
Justus: Dialogues 4.55 says it "happened three years since in mine own Monastery" (Dialogues written about 593-594), so "About 590", not "Before 590".
John the Faster: Letter 7.33 is about his successor Cyriacus (John died 595). The "precursor of Antichrist" line is now introduced "After John died, he told the emperor".

Maximus (Letter 4.47): he was ordained against the EMPEROR's orders ("after the most serene Lord the Emperor had sent orders that he should not be ordained"); the letter is to Sabinian, Gregory's envoy.
Letter 8.30: "my honour is the honour of the universal Church: my honour is the solid vigour of my brethren" - page no longer says "the honour of his brother bishops".

Mary Magdalene: 22 July has been a feast, not a memorial, since 2016; page now says "its day for her". Homily 33 line checked in Migne PL 76 ("Hanc vero quam Lucas peccatricem mulierem, Joannes Mariam nominat...").

Silvia: Britannica "took vows on the death of her husband"; Dudden vol. 1: "After the death of Gordianus she embraced a life of seclusion ... at a place called Cella Nova, close by the great door of the Basilica of St. Paul". Cite now names both. Tarsilla: Dialogues 4.16 says she lived "in the company of two others of her sisters"; nothing says "in their own house".

Sabinian: Dudden's summary of Paul's Life 29: three times "with mild reproof exhorted him to act more generously", then "violently rebuked and threatened him, and finally struck him a blow on the head".

In art: CE "tiara and double cross. A dove is his special emblem"; the dove sits on his head with its beak at his lips, not "at his ear". Letters: "many of his letters open with" servus servorum Dei (Barmby prints most salutations as "Gregory to X, &c."; John the Deacon says he began his letters so).
Chant: Britannica's own page states it flatly ("named for St. Gregory I, who codified and collected the chant"); "still repeats it", not "tells it as tradition".
Type note: Dialogues 1 preface says "a solitary place", not "quiet".
Feasts note: the Calendarium (1969) gives only "Cum autem haec dies semper incidat in Quadragesima"; the added gloss "when saints' memorials are not kept" is dropped.
